analysis.one_liner: Bans the import, manufacture, and sale of asbestos-containing products and expands federal research on asbestos diseases.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Steve Cohen with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittees and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most Americans assume asbestos is banned, but the bill's findings show the U.S. still imported and used about 2,000 metric tons of asbestos in 2006, mostly in roofing products and coatings, plus more than $100 million a year in brake parts [S3]. The bill would direct the EPA to write rules prohibiting importing, manufacturing, processing, or distributing asbestos-containing products, with limited exemptions by petition and open-ended exemptions for the Defense Department and NASA, and would require disposal of products in the supply chain within two years [S2]. It would also fund a public education campaign about asbestos dangers and expand federal research and treatment networks for mesothelioma and other asbestos diseases [S2]. The bill never advanced past committee referral [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families exposed to asbestos on the job and at home, consumers who buy products like brakes and roofing without knowing asbestos is inside, and patients with mesothelioma and other asbestos diseases who would benefit from new research and treatment networks [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits importing, manufacturing, processing, or distributing asbestos-containing products, closing the gap left when a court struck down the EPA's 1989 phase-out rules [S2] [S3].

Funds a national research and treatment network for mesothelioma and other asbestos-related diseases, including at least 10 treatment centers and $10 million per year for fiscal years 2008 through 2012, plus Defense Department research aimed at veterans, about a third of whom make up mesothelioma victims exposed on Navy ships and in shipyards [S3].
Creates a public education program warning consumers and workers about asbestos dangers in homes and workplaces and informing patients about treatments and clinical trials [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and importers of asbestos-containing products, including makers of roofing products, coatings, and brake parts, would have to stop using asbestos and find substitutes within two years, and businesses holding such products in the stream of commerce would have to dispose of them [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill carves out unreviewed, unlimited-duration exemptions for Department of Defense and NASA uses, so asbestos would remain in use for military and space applications if those agencies certify it is necessary [S3].
Businesses would bear the cost of replacing asbestos in products and disposing of stock within two years, which could raise prices for products like brakes and roofing in the transition [S2] [S3].
The EPA could grant petitions for continued use of up to one year at a time, giving regulated companies a recurring route to seek exceptions to the ban [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: the bill's findings state there is no known safe level of asbestos exposure and cite estimates of as many as 10,000 American deaths per year from asbestos-related diseases [S3]. The main costs fall on a small set of manufacturers and importers who would need substitutes, and the transition window is short at two years [S2]. The military and NASA exemptions mean the ban would not be complete, but for consumer and industrial products it would largely match bans already in force in 40 other countries [S3].

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and two of its subcommittees on the same day, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Ban Asbestos in America Act of 2007 on August 1, 2007 [S5].

It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and to the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials and the Subcommittee on Health, and no committee action, floor vote, or further step followed for the rest of the 110th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and importers of asbestos-containing products avoided a ban and the cost of switching to substitutes; workers and the public gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban asbestos-containing products and fund asbestos-disease research

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never reached a markup or a floor vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever formed in the record [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would prohibit them from importing, making, or selling asbestos-containing products, including the roofing materials, coatings, and brake parts described in the findings, and would require disposal of products in the supply chain within two years [S2] [S3]. Their continued sales depend on consumers and workers bearing exposure risks the bill says have no safe level [S3].

industries.industry: Producers of substitute fibers and minerals
industries.note: A ban would force manufacturers to find substitutes that do not present an unreasonable risk, creating demand for replacement materials [S3].
